Making the impossible marketable

Spiritualist publications warned that mediumship could not be bought. Nevertheless, mediums had livelihoods,

needed subscribers and organisers needed to cover costs. Mediumship was therefore presented as an exhausting and often dangerous duty whose selfless practitioners deserved to be paid fairly for their services.

To protect the movement’s brand, mediums such as Daniel Dunglas Home would

refuse direct payment for seances. Instead, he accepted gifts, hospitality, travel opportunities and material support from wealthy patrons, while other mediums requested expenses and a moderate fee proportionate to their clients’ means.

became easier to accept when presented as support for a higher calling.

The same tension appeared in spiritualist publishing. Periodicals such as the Medium and Daybreak could devote their opening pages to condemning materialism and warning readers against excessive attachment to worldly

, only to fill their back pages with advertisements for dubious remedies, elixirs and quasi-scientific products marketed to those very readers. Spiritualism’s critique of consumer culture actually helped generate further opportunities for consumption.

Scientific credibility also required

. Spiritualists welcomed scientists’ involvement, approximated scientific and philosophical language, and used technical equipment to make extraordinary claims appear worthy of serious attention.

The ghosts of Victorian capitalism still haunt us

The Victorian fascination with communicating beyond the grave may seem distant from our technologically sophisticated present. Yet

forms of “digital necromancy” reveal a remarkably familiar tension: the desire to transcend the limits of human existence continues to generate new income streams.

As with Victorian mediums, today’s grief-tech entrepreneurs operate within a delicate relationship between

need, technological credibility and commercial legitimacy. The promise of connection may be sincerely offered and deeply meaningful to those who seek it, even as that same promise becomes a source of profit.

questions.prompt: Which statement best summarises the overall focus of this article?
options: Anticipating problems at work can create stress even before those problems occur.
Shopping early can provide practical benefits for both consumers and retailers.
State responses to childcare funding cuts offer lessons for future policy.
Victorian spiritualism turned the desire to communicate beyond death into commercial opportunities.

questions.evidence: Spiritualism offered an escape from Victorian commercial culture while drawing people into new forms of consumption.
